passages.happening:
The chapter opens with two commands the book has given before: no idols, and “You must keep My Sabbaths and have reverence for My sanctuary” (verse 2).

Then the promises. “If you follow My statutes and carefully keep My commandments, I will give you rains in their season, and the land will yield its produce” (verses 3-4). There will be food in plenty, peace in the land, and safety from enemies and wild animals (verses 5-10).

“And I will make My dwelling place among you, and My soul will not despise you. I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be My people” (verses 11-12).

“I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt so that you would no longer be slaves to the Egyptians. I broke the bars of your yoke and enabled you to walk in uprightness” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
This chapter closes the laws given at Sinai. In the ancient world, treaties between a great king and the kings under him commonly ended with blessings for keeping faith and curses for breaking it. Hittite treaties did, and so did Assyrian ones. Israel's covenant follows a form its neighbors would have known, with one great difference. The other party is not a human king. It is the LORD.

The blessings begin with rain. The hill country of Canaan had no great river like the Nile. Its farmers lived by the autumn and spring rains. The picture is of harvests so large that threshing runs on into grape-picking, and grape-picking into sowing.

But the promises do not reach their height in food or in safety. They reach it in a person. ‘I will walk among you.’ The Hebrew verb is the one used of God walking in the garden in Genesis 3:8. What was lost in Eden is held out again. This is what the whole book has been for: the offerings, the priests, the washings and the feasts all served this, that God might live with his people.

The last line gives the ground, as so often in Leviticus. These are not terms offered to slaves hoping to win their freedom. They are spoken by the one who has already broken the yoke. The verse says he enabled them to walk upright, like people who no longer bend under a load.
passages.later:
Deuteronomy sets out the same blessings and curses at greater length (Deuteronomy 28).

Ezekiel, in exile, hears the promise renewed: “My dwelling place will be with them; I will be their God, and they will be My people” (Ezekiel 37:27).

Paul quotes it to the church: “I will dwell with them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be My people” (2 Corinthians 6:16). And the Bible's last vision sees it kept: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them” (Revelation 21:3).
passages.asks: The greatest promise in the list is not rain or peace but God's own company. Ask what you most want from God, and whether it is him or only what he gives. And ask what yoke he has already broken for you, and whether you are walking upright or still bent as if it were there.

passages.happening:
“If, however, you fail to obey Me and to carry out all these commandments”, and so break the covenant, trouble will come (verses 14-15): sickness, defeat, and crops eaten by enemies (verses 16-17).

Four more times the text says, in effect, and if you still will not listen. Each time the trouble grows: drought, with a sky ‘like iron’ (verse 19); wild animals (verse 22); sword, plague and hunger inside besieged cities (verses 25-26); and at the last the horrors of a long siege, ruined towns, and the people scattered among the nations (verses 29-33).

“Then the land shall enjoy its Sabbaths all the days it lies desolate, while you are in the land of your enemies” (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
The warnings are much longer than the promises, and they are hard to read. They come in five rising steps. Each begins with a condition: if after all this you will not obey. The number seven marks each step.

That shape matters. These are not five punishments falling at once. Between each step and the next there is a pause, a chance to turn. Verse 23 names what the troubles are for: ‘discipline’. The Hebrew verb is the one Proverbs uses for a father teaching his son. The aim at every step is to bring Israel back before the next one comes.

A rare Hebrew word runs through this half, translated ‘hostility’. Israel walks against God, and God answers by walking against Israel. The relationship has become a collision.

Verse 29 is the most terrible line in the book. It describes what hunger did to people in a city under long siege. It is not something God approves or commands. It is a warning, set down in advance, of where the road ends. The Bible records with grief that it happened, in Samaria and in Jerusalem.

And there is a bitter justice in verses 34 and 35. Israel was told to rest the land every seventh year. If it would not, the land would have its rest anyway, empty, while the people were far away.

It matters who is being spoken to. These words are addressed to Israel as a nation, living in its land under the covenant made at Sinai. They describe the long direction of a people's life together over generations.
passages.later:
Israel's own writers read their history by this chapter. Of the exile in Babylon, Chronicles says, “So the land enjoyed its Sabbath rest all the days of the desolation” (2 Chronicles 36:21).

Lamentations weeps over the siege of Jerusalem in words that recall verse 29 (Lamentations 4:10).

Proverbs speaks of discipline as this chapter does: “for the LORD disciplines the one He loves, as does a father the son in whom he delights” (Proverbs 3:12).
passages.hard:
Does this chapter mean that suffering is God's punishment, and that people who are well off are being rewarded?

No. And because the chapter has been used to say so, it has to be answered carefully.

The chapter does link obedience with blessing and rebellion with disaster. But it speaks to Israel as a nation in its land under the covenant of Sinai. It describes where a whole people's life is heading over time. It is not a rule for reading any one person's life.

The rest of the Bible refuses to read it that way. Job suffers though God himself calls him ‘blameless and upright’ (Job 1:8). Many psalms cry out over the suffering of the innocent. When people told Jesus of men killed by a ruler, and of eighteen killed when a tower fell, he asked, “Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem?”, and answered, “No, I tell you” (Luke 13:4-5). When his disciples asked whose sin had made a man blind, he said, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned” (John 9:3). And the New Testament does not promise wealth or health to the faithful. It promises hardship, and God's presence in it.

So this chapter is never God's verdict on your illness, your poverty, your childlessness or your loss. No one should be told that their illness or disability is a punishment. A person who uses these verses to tell a grieving family that they brought it on themselves is misusing them.

One more misuse must be named. For centuries some Christians read chapters like this as God's lasting curse on the Jewish people, and took the sufferings of Jews as proof. That reading is false, and this site rejects it. These are Israel's own Scriptures, in which Israel confesses its own sin, and the chapter ends with God refusing to reject his people. The note on Acts 2:22-28 says more. These notes say nothing against any people, ancient or modern.

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: At each step God paused, and the trouble was meant to turn Israel back. Ask whether there is a warning in your life that you have been walking past. And ask whether you have ever looked at someone else's suffering and quietly decided they deserved it.

passages.happening:
“But if they will confess their iniquity and that of their fathers”, and if their hearts are humbled (verses 40-41), “then I will remember My covenant with Jacob and My covenant with Isaac and My covenant with Abraham, and I will remember the land” (verse 42).

“Yet in spite of this, when they are in the land of their enemies, I will not reject or despise them so as to destroy them and break My covenant with them; for I am the LORD their God” (verse 44).

“But for their sake I will remember the covenant with their fathers, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt in the sight of the nations, that I might be their God. I am the LORD” (verse 45).

“These are the statutes, ordinances, and laws that the LORD established between Himself and the Israelites through Moses on Mount Sinai” (verse 46).
passages.hearers:
The chapter does not end with the curses. It ends with mercy.

Even in exile, even at the last step, the way back stays open. Two things are named. The people confess: their own wrong and their fathers'. And their hearts are humbled. The text speaks of an ‘uncircumcised’ heart. Circumcision was the outward sign of the covenant. An uncircumcised heart is an inner life that has not been given to God.

Then God remembers. In the Bible, God's remembering does not mean he had forgotten. It means he acts on what he has promised. When he remembered Noah, the waters went down.

He names the fathers backward, Jacob, Isaac, Abraham, as though following the covenant down to its root. The promise to Abraham is older than Sinai, and Israel's failure at Sinai cannot cancel it.

Verse 44 is among the most important sentences in the book. Israel can break the covenant (verse 15). God says that he will not. ‘I will not reject or despise them.’ The last word over Israel in Leviticus is that God holds on.

For the people who later lived through the exile, this chapter did two things. It explained their suffering, and it gave them ground to hope.
passages.later:
Moses says the same in Deuteronomy: when the people return to the LORD, “then He will restore you from captivity and have compassion on you” (Deuteronomy 30:3).

In exile, Daniel prayed as verse 40 describes, confessing for himself and his people: “we have sinned and done wrong” (Daniel 9:5).

Paul asks whether God has cast off Israel, and answers from this ground: “did God reject His people? Certainly not!” (Romans 11:1). “For God’s gifts and His call are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29).
passages.asks: Israel could break the covenant; God said he would not. Ask whether you believe that God's hold on you is stronger than your hold on him. And ask what you need to confess, plainly and without excuse, so that you can come home.
